The BGA version relies on the third edition (2026). In the early 16th century, Goa stood at the crossroads of global trade. Situated on India's western coast, the city quickly grew into one of the most important commercial hubs of the Indian Ocean world. Merchants from India, Arabia, Africa, and Europe converged here to exchange spices, textiles, precious goods, and knowledge. Over the course of the game, players develop their trading operations by acquiring ships, securing merchant contracts, expanding plantations, and advancing along several progress tracks. Each round, players participate in auctions to gain access to powerful actions, forcing them to carefully balance short-term needs against long-term growth. Success in Goa comes from timing your investments, adapting to changing market opportunities, and building an efficient economic engine. Multiple paths to victory are available, rewarding flexible strategies and thoughtful planning rather than tactical luck. By the end of the game, the player who has best managed their resources, progress, and influence will emerge as the most successful trading house in Goa. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Components 2 Setup 3 Gameplay Overview 4 On Your Turn 5 End of game 6 Scoring 7 Options 8 Player Preferences Components 1 Game Board (center of the table) with 1 Round Marker 1 Player Board per player : with 5 colored progress markers + 5 colored auction markers 1 Nazar Stone (starting player marker) displayed on player side panel when assigned to a player 29 Market Tiles (Day) - 4 randomly removed 29 Market Tiles (Night) - 4 randomly removed 18 Outposts tiles unlimited currencies cards (Pardaos, Ships, Contracts, Compasses) 30 Exploration Cards unlimited Goods tokens of 5 types/colors Coconut coir Turmeric Pepper Silk Dried fish Setup The game starts with the day phase : 25/29 market tiles randomly placed on the 5x5 grid of the main board; later for the night phase 25/29 other market tiles will be randomly placed on the grid. 1 Exploration Card is drawn by each player until one player draw an Elephant symbol and becomes the starting player with 5 money, the others with 10. Gameplay Overview A game of Goa is divided into day and night cycles, each of which consists of 4 rounds. After the day cycle, remove all tiles from the playing area and setup the night tiles on the instead. At the end of the night cycle, the game ends and the player with the most points is declared the winner. Each round consists of 3 successive steps : 1. Place Auction Markers 2. Tile Auctions 3. Actions On Your Turn Step 1. Place Auction Markers : Each player places an auction marker on the grid. The first player places an auction marker and the starting player token on an empty space. Then each player places an auction marker next to the previous marker if possible. Step 2. Tile Auctions : Each player, starting with the player after the one who auctioned that tile/token has 1 turn to decide if they want to overbid or pass the auction related to the spots. The first auction is to gain the starting player marker + 1 compass card. All others are to gain the tile under the auction marker. The last player in the sequence (the same one who placed their auction marker on that tile/token) has these choices: They may accept the highest bid. The player with that bid pays the player who auctioned the tile. They may take the tile for themselves. The player pays 1 less than the highest bid to the supply. If no one bid anything, they may take the tile for free. Step 3. Actions : each player must play 1 possible action + max 1 card from their hand + play tiles from their hand until everyone played 3 actions. [Rating: 1/10] Long game that has almost too much to do. The strategic horizon can be very limited and paths to victory are hard to plot. Extra actions are a necessity in order to progress, so they become the touchstone and I would bet that there is a clear correlation of players with more actions receiving higher scores. It seems like such a general and unforgiving necessity that to lose out on gaining extra actions leaves a player with limited options. Also, it is *very* difficult to figure out who to bid against because it is hard to determine who is leading.

[Rating: 1/10] I am aware that I am against the overwhelming majority here. But this game is not only WAY too abstract for my taste, it also lacks (almost) any means of interaction, with the exception of that awfully awkward auction. Furthermore I fail to see how the game-mechanics are related to what the game is supposed to simulate. This is a game about game mechanics, not about building a colonial enterprise. Thus, if you like abstract games with low interaction and pointracing, this will be your game. Otherwise, if you prefer sophisticated simulations with a high amount of flavour and interaction: Beware

[Rating: 1/10] Interesting bidding mechanics.  Decent game, but the theme just doesn't do it for me.  Seems to take much longer than it should.

[Rating: 1.5/10] 2 solo plays  I expected a MPS core with an added auction, but it was even a little bit less interactive than expected. And rigid. Firstly the once around auction is too controlled and I just don't see a reason behind its logic. The engine building part is also fairly static: just tick the boxes (a.k.a. tech three). It falls somewhere in a similar feel as hansa Teitonica, and yet that one is less balanced, a bit more interactive and hence a tad more interesting.   Better than worker placements though.  The theme, ehm, what theme, is there a theme? The spice bags pieces are cute and that's it.

[Rating: 2/10] mmm... you play a solo game with friends. the worst part is that I've not seen the spirit. You can call it Goa or Minsk or Math4Dummy.

[Rating: 2/10] I've just not been all that impressed after a few plays.  Just seems that there are better options out there to play than this.  I can't stand the once around the table auction.  If you are unlucky enough to be put to the right of the guy that always bids 1 over you, might as well not play.  Well, according to the ratings "2 extremely annoying game won't play this ever again" is accurate for me.  I've passed up many chances to play this because I can't stand it.
